newsitem.title: USA: Clinton has minor ills compared with predecessors.
newsitem.headline: Clinton has minor ills compared with predecessors.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's torn knee tendon is a minor problem compared with his predecessors' brushes with the scalpel and their other ailments.
Doctors said Clinton, 50, would be given a local anaesthetic and remain conscious during surgery to fix a torn tendon at nearby Bethesda Naval Hospital on Friday.
Clinton's immediate predecessor, George Bush, spent time in the hospital in May 1991 for an erratic heart rhythm traced to an overactive thyroid condition known as Graves' disease.
And in January 1992, Bush, then 67, collapsed at a formal state dinner in Japan after what he called a bout with a "24-hour bug" that was more embarassing diplomatically than medically significant.
Barely three months after taking office in 1981 at age 69, Ronald Reagan was nearly killed by a lone gunman. Doctors removed a bullet lodged in the left lower lobe of his lung.

Reagan, the oldest president to take office when he was sworn in, underwent major surgery again on July 13, 1985 for removal of a cancerous growth in his large intestine. In 1986, he had two small benign polyps removed.
George Washington, the first president, nearly died in office from pneumonia and from complications caused by a carbuncle inflamation on his left thigh.
Throughout U.S. history, White House aides have covered up or played down presidential illnesses to avoid any crisis of confidence and to protect any reelection prospects.
For instance, John Kennedy, 43 when he entered the White House in 1961, kept hidden that he suffered from Addison's Disease, a treatable disorder of the adrenal glands.

Thrust into the presidency by Kennedy's assassination, Lyndon Johnson had already had a heart attack five years earlier. During his presidency, he suffered a gall bladder attack and underwent major surgery.

Richard Nixon, who suffered from chronic phlebitis, a vein inflamation, was determined by a three-doctor panel to be too ill to testify at the Watergate conspiracy trial after he became the first president to resign office in 1974.
Franklin Roosevelt, a polio victim who was the only president to be reelected three times, died in office on April 12, 1945 after a massive cerebral haemorrhage.

Woodrow Wilson's massive stroke in late 1919 left the country without a functioning chief executive until his term ended in 1921. His successor, Warren Harding, had high blood pressure and heart disease when he was elected and died in office in 1923.

Chester Arthur, 50 when he took office in 1881, suffered from Bright's disease, an incurable kidney disorder. Grover Cleveland, 47 when he entered the White House in 1885, underwent surgery to remove a cancerous growth in his mouth. In an effort to avoid roiling financial markets, Cleveland's operation was reported as a "tooth extraction."

On occasion, presidents have received questionable medical care. When Dwight Eisenhower suffered a heart attack in Denver in 1955, his doctor told the president's wife, Mamie, to get back into bed with her husband to keep him warm and delayed sending Eisenhower to a hospital for most of the day.
Clinton, a hardy jogger and golf enthusiast, had his last brush with the surgeon's knife on Sept. 4, 1996, when an apparently benign cyst was removed from his neck in a minor 12-minute operation.
He told an interviewer during his re-election campaign last year that he had never had a serious illness and had controlled his three most annoying health problems: hoarseness, allergies and weight.
